## What Inverse Dynamics Can Identify

With a declared mechanical model, mass properties, motion derivatives and known external loads, inverse dynamics estimates the net generalized input needed to reproduce that motion. It already accounts for gravity and inertial coupling. Control-affine analysis reorganizes the same equations and supplies explicit interventions; it does not recover a missing input by subtracting gravity a second time.

What remains difficult is identifying the physiological source of that input. Multiple muscle recruitment patterns, bilateral hand-force distributions and impedance states can be compatible with the same motion. Separating those possibilities requires additional evidence.

## From Generalized Torque to Actuator Input

If $Bu=\tau_{\mathrm{ID}}$ and $B$ has full column rank, a consistent load has a unique input, $u=B^+\tau_{\mathrm{ID}}$. First check that $BB^+\tau_{\mathrm{ID}}=\tau_{\mathrm{ID}}$: a residual indicates inconsistency or noise, not an identified hidden muscle.

With redundant actuators, $u=B^+\tau_{\mathrm{ID}}+n$ for $n\in\ker B$. Muscle nonnegativity, force–length/velocity properties, activation dynamics and independent measurements restrict this family. A minimum-norm solution is an assumption about allocation, not an observation of the nervous system.

An inverse-dynamics implementation that omits passive tissue forces estimates a net joint load that includes them. A model that explicitly subtracts those forces estimates a different residual input. Declare that boundary before comparing results. This is especially important when impedance was identified from an actively contracting subject.

## Why the Mechanisms Are Intertwined

Earlier muscle work changes segment motion and shaft deformation. The resulting state changes current gravitational leverage, inertial coupling and the effect of a new torque. A force can redirect club motion with little power in its normal direction, while another component supplies work. The complete wrench power must be calculated before inferring energy transfer.

A zero-input branch answers what a specified model predicts after one declared intervention. It does not establish what a golfer would feel, whether a motion is effortless, or which coaching cue improves it. A frozen-impedance branch and a muscle-relaxation experiment are different interventions.

## An Evidence-Driven Analysis

1. Define the question and measured outcome: net grip wrench, club speed, segment energy, or a tissue-specific load.
2. State the model boundary, coordinate conventions, external loads and passive-force treatment.
3. Propagate motion, force, parameter and filtering uncertainty into the inferred quantities.
4. Check forward/inverse consistency and analytic limits before making a same-state attribution.
5. Test whether conclusions survive alternative contact, muscle and shaft models.
6. Use independent measurements to assess external validity. Agreement between two rearrangements of the same equations establishes consistency only.

A useful falsifier is a model that reproduces the measured motion but predicts hand forces outside independent measurement uncertainty. Another is a sign or ranking of an attribution that reverses under plausible parameter changes. Report such outcomes rather than presenting a mechanically possible explanation as the unique cause.

## In Plain Language

Watching a car travel down a hill does not reveal engine effort from speed alone. Given acceleration, slope, mass and resistance, ordinary mechanics can estimate the net driving force. It still cannot tell how the driver produced that force or how hard the driver felt they were working. The golf-swing distinction is the same: net mechanical input can be estimated under a model; muscle recruitment, sensation and strategy need further evidence.
